lesson.title: Levers and pulleys

lead.text: A lever is a rigid bar that turns about a fixed point called the fulcrum. Think of a crowbar prying up a heavy lid. The fulcrum is the point where the bar rests on the ground. Your hand supplies the effort, the force you apply. The lid pushes back with the load, the force you are working against.

You met moments earlier in the course: a force times its distance from the pivot. A lever held at rest has its moments balanced about the fulcrum, so effort × effort arm = load × load arm, where each arm is the distance from the fulcrum to where that force acts. Say the lid pushes back with 600 N at 0.1 m from the fulcrum, and your hand is 0.5 m from it. The moments balance when effort × 0.5 = 600 × 0.1, so the effort is 60 ÷ 0.5 = 120 N.
The spanner works the same way. The nut needs a fixed turning effect, and a longer arm supplies it with less force.
The nut needs the same turning effect whichever spanner you use.

The ratio of the load to the effort tells you how much a lever multiplies your force. It is called mechanical advantage, MA = load ÷ effort. In the prying example the effort is 120 N for a 600 N load, so MA = 600 ÷ 120 = 5. Because effort × effort arm = load × load arm, the same number comes from the arms: MA = effort arm ÷ load arm = 0.5 ÷ 0.1 = 5.

A mechanical advantage above 1 means the lever gives out more force than you put in. It does not give out more energy. The long arm moves through a bigger distance than the short one, and you pay for the extra force with extra distance. The end of this lesson comes back to that cost.
Use the ratio of the arms that you have just met.

steps.headline: A 2 m bar balances an 800 N load 0.25 m from the fulcrum, with the effort at the far end. Find the effort.

lead.text: Here is the whole method, line by line.

workedSteps.text: Work out the load's moment, then divide by the effort arm.

steps.headline: The crowbar's handle is 1.2 m from the fulcrum and the 900 N load is 0.2 m from it. Find the effort.

lead.text: The method is the same as in the worked example.

lead.text: So far the fulcrum has sat between your hand and the load. That is one of three arrangements, named by which of the three points, fulcrum, load or effort, lies in the middle. Each arrangement is called a lever class.

A first-class lever has the fulcrum in the middle, as on a seesaw or a crowbar. With the load in the middle, as in a nutcracker or a bottle opener, the lever is second class, and its effort arm is longer than its load arm, so the effort is smaller than the load. Put the effort in the middle and the lever is third class. Its effort arm is shorter than its load arm, so the effort has to be larger than the load. That looks like a loss, but it buys speed and reach, because a small movement of the effort gives a large movement of the load. The picture shows one of each.

afterFigure.text: Your forearm is a third-class lever. The elbow is the fulcrum. The biceps pulls a short distance from it, with a weight in your hand at the far end. If the biceps acts at one seventh of the distance from the elbow to the hand, it must pull with seven times the weight you hold. The same moment balance as for the crowbar gives the answer.

lead.text: Find which of the three points sits between the other two.

steps.headline: Pulleys and the block and tackle

lead.text: A pulley is a wheel with a groove for a rope. One fixed pulley only changes the direction of the pull. Mount several pulleys in two blocks, one fixed and one moving with the load. Run one continuous rope through them all. That arrangement is a block and tackle.

Ignoring friction, one rope has the same tension all along it. Each strand that supports the moving block pulls on it with that tension, and the tension is the effort you pull with. The supporting strands share the load, so with n of them, effort = load ÷ n. A 500 N load on 2 strands needs 250 N, and on 5 strands it needs 100 N, so the mechanical advantage is the number of strands. Count only the strands that attach to the moving block or run round it. The picture shows both.
The supporting strands share the load equally.

A lever or pulley that cuts the force must cost something, and the cost is distance. In an ideal machine the work you put in equals the work done on the load. Work is a force times the distance it moves, measured in joules. Take the 5-strand tackle lifting a 500 N load by 0.4 m. The work done on the load is 500 × 0.4 = 200 J.

The effort is 100 N, so for 100 N × distance to make 200 J you must pull 2 m of rope. A direct count agrees. Lifting the block 0.4 m shortens each of the 5 supporting strands by 0.4 m, and all that rope has to come out through your hands: 5 × 0.4 = 2 m. A lever behaves the same way, because the long end swings through a longer arc than the short end. A gain in force is always paid for in distance and never in work.
Every supporting strand gets shorter by the height of the lift, and the rope it gives up passes through your hands.

lesson.orientation: Trade distance for force with levers and rope systems, and count what it costs.

blocks.text: A wheel nut on a car is stuck. A short spanner will not shift it, no matter how hard you push. Someone fetches the long spanner from the boot and the nut comes off with a steady push. You did not get stronger, and the nut did not change.

The first half of this course was about structures that stay still, where forces and moments balance. A spanner works by the same balance with one difference: you choose where to put your hand, and the balance rewards you for choosing well. Machines that multiply a force are built around that idea.

This lesson looks at two of the simplest machines for multiplying a force: a bar that turns about a point, and a rope run over wheels. It finds how much force each needs and sorts the bars into three kinds. It ends with the price you pay for the saving.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the effort a lever or pulley needs for a load, and see what it costs you in distance.

recap.keyIdea: A lever balances effort × effort arm against load × load arm, and a pulley with n strands divides the load by n. Both trade distance for force.

blocks.text: Back at the spanner, a longer arm meant less force for the same turning effect. A crowbar with a 1.2 m handle and a 0.2 m load arm has a mechanical advantage of 6, so it holds 900 N with 150 N. A 4-strand pulley holds 800 N with 200 N, but you pull 2 m of rope to lift the load 0.5 m.

recap.nextHook: Levers and pulleys trade distance for force. Gears do the same job for something that spins, and the next lesson shows how the number of teeth sets the speed.

questions.prompt: A stuck nut needs a 100 N push on a short spanner. You swap it for a spanner twice as long and still push at the end. What push, in newtons, does the long spanner need?
hints: The nut needs the same turning moment either way.
A moment is force times distance.
Twice the distance needs half the force.
questions.onCorrect: 50 N. The same turning moment with twice the arm needs half the force. That is the lever.

misconceptions.feedback: A longer spanner means less force, not more, for the same moment.
That is the push with the short spanner. A longer arm needs less force.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The moment is fixed: 100 N × d. With 2d, the force is 100 ÷ 2 = 50 N.

questions.prompt: Which gives a lever the greater mechanical advantage?
hints: MA is the effort arm divided by the load arm.
questions.onCorrect: MA is effort arm over load arm, so lengthening the effort arm raises it.

misconceptions.feedback: A longer load arm lowers the ratio, since the load arm is the divisor.
The load does not change the ratio of the arms. It changes the effort needed.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A longer effort arm. MA = effort arm ÷ load arm, so a longer effort arm raises it.

questions.prompt: A crowbar is levered over a fulcrum. The hand pushes 1.2 m from the fulcrum and the load sits 0.2 m from it. Find the mechanical advantage.
hints: Mechanical advantage is load force over effort force.
For a balanced lever, that equals the ratio of the arms.
Calculate 1.2 ÷ 0.2.
questions.onCorrect: 6: the effort arm is six times the load arm, so the load force is six times the effort.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the arms. Mechanical advantage is a ratio.
That is the ratio upside down. Here the effort arm is the longer one.

questions.prompt: Why do the moments about the fulcrum balance?
hints: What is the net moment on a body at rest?
questions.onCorrect: At rest, the moments cancel about any point. Choosing the fulcrum removes the unknown force there.

misconceptions.feedback: The arms usually differ, and that difference is what gives mechanical advantage.
The effort and load differ too. Only their moments match.

choices.label: The lever is held at rest, so its net moment is zero.
Because the two arms are always equal.
Because the effort always equals the load.

acceptedIdeas: The lever is held at rest, so its net moment is zero.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The lever is held at rest, so its net moment is zero.. At rest the net moment is zero, so effort × effort arm equals load × load arm.

hints: Divide the load's moment by the effort arm.
The load's moment is 180 N·m.
Calculate 180 ÷ 1.2.
questions.onCorrect: 150 N holds a 900 N load: the long arm trades distance for force.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by the mechanical advantage. A lever reduces the effort needed.
That is the load. The effort is smaller, because the long arm helps.

questions.prompt: In tweezers, the effort is applied between the fulcrum and the load. Which class of lever is that?
hints: Which of the three points is in the middle?
questions.onCorrect: Effort in the middle makes a third-class lever, which gives up force for speed and reach.

misconceptions.feedback: First class has the fulcrum in the middle, like a seesaw.
Second class has the load in the middle, like a nutcracker.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Third class. Effort in the middle is a third-class lever.

questions.prompt: A pulley system has 4 rope strands supporting the moving block, which carries an 800 N load. Ignoring friction and the block's weight, find the effort in newtons.
hints: The rope tension is the same in every strand.
The supporting strands share the load equally.
Calculate 800 ÷ 4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each of the 4 strands carries the rope tension: effort = 800 ÷ 4 = 200 N.

questions.onCorrect: 200 N: the supporting strands share the load, so the effort is the load divided by their number.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by the number of strands. They share the load, so divide.
That is the load, not the effort. The strands share it.

questions.prompt: To lift an 800 N load 0.5 m with 4 supporting strands, how many metres of rope must be pulled?
hints: Every supporting strand gets shorter by the lift height.
The rope taken up comes out through the hand.
Calculate 4 × 0.5.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each strand shortens by 0.5 m: 4 × 0.5 = 2 m.

questions.onCorrect: 2 m: four strands each shorten by the lift. Less force costs more rope.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides. Every strand shortens by the lift, so multiply by the number of strands.
That is the lift. The rope pulled through is more than that.

questions.prompt: In the forearm, the biceps attaches 0.04 m from the elbow, and a 50 N weight is held in the hand 0.32 m from the elbow. Treating the forearm as a weightless horizontal lever, find the biceps force in newtons.
hints: The elbow is the fulcrum.
Balance moments: effort × effort arm = load × load arm.
Calculate 50 × 0.32 ÷ 0.04.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Biceps × 0.04 = 50 × 0.32, so the biceps pulls 16 ÷ 0.04 = 400 N, eight times the weight held.

questions.onCorrect: 400 N: here the effort arm is the short one, so the effort is larger than the load.

misconceptions.feedback: That inverts the ratio. The effort arm is the shorter arm, so the effort must be the larger force.
That is the weight's moment about the elbow in N·m. Divide by the biceps arm to get a force.

questions.prompt: A wheelbarrow has its load between the wheel axle and the handles. Which class of lever is it: first, second or third?
hints: Locate the fulcrum first, then see which of load and effort lies between.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Second class: the load sits between the fulcrum and the effort.

questions.onCorrect: The load sits between the fulcrum and the effort: second class.

misconceptions.feedback: A first-class lever has the fulcrum in the middle, like a seesaw.
A third-class lever has the effort in the middle. In a wheelbarrow the effort is at the handles, at the end.

questions.prompt: A pulley system has 3 strands supporting the moving block, which carries a 900 N load. Ignoring friction and the block's weight, find the effort in newtons.
hints: The rope tension is the same in every strand.
The supporting strands share the load equally.
Calculate 900 ÷ 3.
questions.onCorrect: 300 N: the load divided by the number of supporting strands.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by the number of strands. They share the load, so divide.
That is the load. The strands share it.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each of the 3 strands carries the rope tension: effort = 900 ÷ 3 = 300 N.
